transcript:
Meeting header
Date/Time: 2025-09-03 15:00 PDT
Duration: 1:15
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Natarajan (Redwood SE), Diego Flores (Redwood SRE advocate), Jordan Lee (Constellation CTO), Maya Rivera (ML Eng), Samir Patel (Platform), Lina Ho (Product)

Summary (auto): quick calibration workshop to align on apples-to... sorry, alignment methodology for throughput and latency benchmarks across on-prem and hosted modes. Focus: Kv cache warm vs cold behavior, batching tradeoffs, quantization reproducibility, and how to make an "apples in different orchards" comparison that the infra team will trust.

Links shared: deck: https://redwood.link/throughput-calibration-deck , benchmark harness repo: https://git.redwood.ai/benchmarks/throughput-harness , example spreadsheet: https://sheets.redwood.ai/constellation-benchmarks

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00:05] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for squeezing this in. quick agenda — align on the benchmark matrix, go over the prompt set design, then run through load patterns and what warm vs cold KV cache measurements mean for Constellation's workloads.
[00:00:22] Jordan: sounds good. we — we mainly care about tail latency p95/p99 during steady state and under burst, and costs as tokens/sec. also want to verify that on-prem numbers match what you show in the hosted docs.
[00:00:40] Priya: great. one quick clarification, when you say on-prem do you mean fully air-gapped hardware or a VPC-connected colo?
[00:00:48] Samir: currently it'll be VPC peered colo cluster with private connections, but some teams will want an air-gapped option later. for this run, VPC peering is fine.
[00:01:00] Diego: okay, that makes the networking part simpler — we can use the same tcp windowing assumptions, lower jitter.
[00:01:12] Lina: also, heads up, our product team will use streaming responses for the UI so we care about first-token latency as well as total token latency.
[00:01:25] Priya: perfect, we'll measure first-byte and token throughput.

[00:02:00] Jordan: question on prompt sets — we have slightly different prompt lengths, some 32 tokens, some 512. do you recommend separating by length?
[00:02:15] Alex: yes separate buckets: short (<64), mid (64-256), long (>256). that lets us see where batching helps vs where kv cache dominates.
[00:02:30] Priya: and also importantly, warm vs cold: if you're doing a chat workload where the KV cache is warm (i.e., previous conversation state cached), latency and throughput change dramatically. so benchmarks must include both cold-start (empty cache) and warm-start (preloaded KV state).
[00:02:50] Maya: when you say preloaded, how deterministic is that? like, do we replay the same prefix to warm the cache?
[00:03:00] Priya: good call — the harness supports prefix-replay. we recommend replaying the last 4 turns or up to X tokens until the KV cache is populated, then measure. note: different tokenization across models can change the effective prefix length.
[00:03:20] Speaker 1: hmm, tokenizer weirdness is a godsend for unexpected results.
[00:03:30] Jordan: ha. okay. what's Redwood's approach to getting apples-to-apples across quantized and full-precision runs?
[00:03:40] Alex: two parts — first, fix the random seed and model version, second, define an exact pipeline: same tokenizer, same stopping criteria, same sampling params (topk, temp, etc). for quantization we run an evaluation set to measure quality delta (exact-match or embedding similarity) and only compare latency/cost on models that meet your quality floor.
[00:04:05] Priya: and we capture logits-level divergence metrics as well as perceptual evals (prompt-specific checks). sometimes int8 has tiny noun swaps — we flag those.
[00:04:20] Maya: ok that makes sense. how do you handle batch sizes? our UI uses concurrency of N=12 per instance typically.
[00:04:30] Diego: for throughput tests we vary concurrent requests and per-request batch size. Redwood's runtime has both request-level batching and internal micro-batching — the harness exposes both knobs. we also track tail latency per model variant.
[00:04:48] Jordan: do you instrument KV cache hit rate? we want to correlate hit rate with cost savings.
[00:04:55] Priya: yes we emit hit/miss counts, cache TTLs, and token-level hit ratios in the telemetry. we can export to your prometheus or push to the console.
[00:05:12] Samir: on the VPC side, what network egress do you expect? we have limited peering bandwidth during business hours.
[00:05:22] Alex: we recommend running loadgen from within the same VPC where possible; for peered testing we'll provide a config that throttles to realistic egress caps and simulates cross-AZ latency.
[00:05:35] Lina: what's the plan for warm-up before measuring?
[00:05:40] Priya: default warm-up: 10 minutes at target QPS or until key metrics stabilize (p95 change <5% over two windows). for cache warm benchmarks, we do a targeted prefix load then a short warm ramp.
[00:05:58] Jordan: ok. can we talk about quantization options? int8 vs int4 vs vanillla fp16?
[00:06:10] Alex: fp16 is the simplest and preserves quality. int8 gives the best speed and memory gains on supported kernels, but you need to validate quality. int4 is aggressive — good for batched throughput on high concurrency workloads but has highest risk of hallucinations on some prompts.
[00:06:30] Maya: have you done any specific tests where int8 changed downstream QA metrics?
[00:06:36] Priya: yes — for a summarization workload we saw a 2-3% ROUGE drop int8 vs fp16; for many generative tasks it's smaller. the harness includes a regression test suite you can plug in.
[00:06:52] Speaker 2: is that the bench regression harness linked earlier?
[00:06:56] Alex: yep, that's the one.

[00:07:30] Priya: demoing the harness quickly — (screen share noise) — on the left you choose the model variant, on the right you choose the prompt set buckets and warm/cold flags, and below you set load profile: steady, sawtooth bursts, or poisson arrivals.
[00:07:55] Maya: do you recommend poisson for realistic traffic?
[00:07:59] Priya: yes, Poisson or measured traces from your prod logs. Poisson is good for synthetic baseline; measured traces are best for fidelity.
[00:08:12] Jordan: what about batch sizing policy? is it latency-first or throughput-first?
[00:08:20] Diego: we have configurable policies: latency-SLO (caps batch size to minimize added latency) and throughput-max (grow batch size until throughput flattens). for UI-first apps you pick latency-SLO. we can also do adaptive batching per workload.
[00:08:40] Samir: curious about adaptive — does it introduce jitter in p99?
[00:08:45] Priya: it can if not tuned; our adaptive policy uses rolling windows and caps batch growth rate to avoid sudden jitter. we'll include p99 smoothing metrics in the report.

[00:09:30] Jordan: on the measurement side, how do you capture first-token latency for streaming?
[00:09:36] Priya: we measure TTFB (time to first byte) at the transport level and token emission latency inside the runtime. streaming adds complexity because client-side buffering affects observed numbers; we instrument both client and server to separate those effects.
[00:09:55] Lina: do you simulate real browsers? our UI has a websocket-based stream with small chunk sizes.
[00:10:02] Alex: yes we have a websocket client emulator that matches your chunking pattern; we can also provide a simple JS harness you can run locally.

[00:11:00] Maya: i want to make sure comparisons are fair across hardware — A100 vs H100 vs on-prem Ampere-like.
[00:11:10] Priya: absolutely, the config matrix will enumerate GPU type, driver + cuda version, model engine build, and compiler flags. we snapshot environment (nvidia-smi, rocm if applicable), kernel versions, and schedule identical steps. the goal is reproducible runs.
[00:11:35] Jordan: what if we can't match kernel driver versions on-prem?
[00:11:40] Diego: we'll document differences and run sensitivity checks. if driver version affects perf we flag it as an environmental variance. we won't claim parity if they differ.

[00:12:15] Jordan: what's the recommended way to report cost? tokens/sec alone isn't enough.
[00:12:23] Alex: we emit tokens-per-second, GPU utilization, power draw (if accessible), and map to cost per million tokens using your pricing assumptions (on-prem cost model or Redwood hosted rates). we'll produce a cost breakdown per 1M tokens and per 100k inference calls.
[00:12:40] Maya: and include model quality deltas, so stakeholders see tradeoff: e.g., int8 saves 40% cost but reduces exact-match by 1.5%.
[00:12:50] Priya: yes — we produce a Pareto chart of cost vs quality.

[00:13:30] Jordan: about KV cache TTLs — what defaults do you use and what to tune?
[00:13:36] Priya: default TTL is session-scoped; for long-running conversational sessions we keep cache for 30 minutes by default. you can tune by token or conversation count. we also track eviction rates.
[00:13:50] Samir: eviction rates are important because high eviction churn kills throughput. can we surface that?
[00:13:55] Diego: yes, eviction churn and average KV size per conversation are reported. helps size memory.

[00:14:30] Priya: now, walk-through of a sample benchmark plan for you: 1) baseline fp16 on hosted (A100) with short/mid/long buckets, cold and warm cache, steady load 100 qps, poisson bursts 300 qps, measure p50/p95/p99, throughput, GPU util. 2) repeat on H100 and on-prem cluster. 3) run quantized variants and regression tests. 4) produce a packet of CSVs and summary PPT.
[00:15:10] Jordan: timeline?
[00:15:13] Alex: we can run hosted baselines in ~2 days after we get prompts and SLOs; on-prem will need your infra window (~1 week). total end-to-end report in 2-3 weeks.

[00:15:50] Maya: small nit — how do you handle prompt templating where user input size varies?
[00:15:56] Priya: harness supports templated prompts with variable-length substitution fields; we can sample user input lengths according to a distribution you provide.
[00:16:10] Jordan: ok. any gotchas for client-side timeouts? our gateway has 30s timeouts currently.
[00:16:18] Alex: for long responses we advise streaming; otherwise you risk gateway timeouts. we'll test with your gateway config.

[00:17:00] Samir: security question — do you need access to our KMS for encryption tests?
[00:17:06] Alex: no, for the benchmark you don't need to share keys. we'll test with a stubbed KMS and provide instructions for plugging your KMS in in the Private deployment stage. but we will need a network path and, if you want, mutual TLS creds for the peered test.
[00:17:28] Lina: can you also capture audit/logging overhead — i.e., does turning on detailed audit logs change latency?
[00:17:36] Priya: yes, we can run with audit-level off and high and show delta. it's usually small but measurable at high QPS.

[00:18:20] Alex: let's talk about reporting format: CSVs per run, an aggregate dashboard template, and a slide deck with key charts. we'll also include reproducibility steps and raw harness commands.
[00:18:34] Jordan: perfect. can you include your per-route cost breakdown — tokenization, kv cache, compute, and overhead?
[00:18:44] Diego: yes we'll supply token-level cost attribution and link to the console for deeper dives.

[00:19:10] Maya: question: do you benchmark with continuous batching enabled? our prod would benefit from prefix caching rather than big batching.
[00:19:20] Priya: we test both continuous batching and prefix-only caching configs. continuous batching helps throughput but prefix caching is best for low-latency chat. we'll show both.

[00:20:05] (brief hold while screenshare changed)
[00:20:30] Priya: i'm pulling up an example CSV — columns: run_id, model_variant, gpu_type, concurrency, batch_size, kv_warm, p50, p95, p99, tokens_per_second, cache_hit_rate, quality_metric, notes.
[00:20:50] Jordan: nice. will you include the raw prompt+response pairs for quality inspection?
[00:20:56] Alex: we can include sampled pairs, redacted for PII if needed.

[00:21:30] Maya: one more on quantization — do you do per-layer calibration or whole-model quantization?
[00:21:36] Priya: both options available; we usually try per-layer symmetric quantization first and then fallback. the harness records layerwise error so you see hotspots.
[00:21:50] Speaker 1: sometimes layerwise fixes are the secret sauce.

[00:22:30] Jordan: let's call out acceptance criteria — what do we need to sign off a variant?
[00:22:36] Alex: acceptance = meets latency SLO (p95 < X ms), quality delta < Y metric, and cost reduction >= Z% compared to host baseline. we will make these numbers configurable for your team.
[00:22:55] Samir: we will provide SLO numbers after this meeting.

[00:23:30] Priya: ok last bit — benchmarking concurrency scenarios: steady-state QPS, sawtooth burst pattern, Poisson arrivals, and measured trace replay. we'll recommend trace replay for final comparisons.
[00:23:50] Lina: can you run a skeleton test during our maintenance window?
[00:23:55] Alex: yeah we can do a quick smoke during your window next Thursday. i'll send proposed times.

[00:24:30] Jordan: any concerns about reproducibility over time? we want to re-run quarterly and compare.
[00:24:36] Priya: all runs are hashed with environment snapshot and random seeds; we store the harness config so you can re-run and get comparable results.

[00:25:10] Maya: small question — if we change tokenization (e.g., different tokenizer or pre-tokenize on client) how do you adjust?
[00:25:18] Priya: we include tokenizer in the snapshot and provide the tokenized counts. if you pre-tokenize, you should feed the harness the exact tokenized inputs.

[00:26:00] (tangential discussion about infra windows and who to cc)
[00:28:10] Alex: recap — Redwood sends harness + load generator, Constellation sends prompt sets and SLOs, coordinate on VPC peering window, run hosted baseline then on-prem, Redwood to deliver report.
[00:28:30] Jordan: sounds good.

[00:29:00] (closing remarks, some small talk about conference attendance)

[01:14:30] Alex: ok thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the repo link and calendar invites for the smoke test. bye.
[01:14:40] Jordan: thanks, bye.

--- End of transcript ---
